intro: How the client, the server and the data layer fit together.

entries.short: DNS, edge, balancer, server, data, back.
entries.medium: DNS resolves the name, a CDN or edge may answer from cache, a load balancer routes to a healthy instance, the handler runs, data is read from cache or database, and the response travels back.
entries.detail: Each hop is a place to cache, time out, retry or fail. Knowing the path is how you locate latency.

entries.medium: The client holds an opaque id in a cookie and the state lives on the server, usually in a shared store so any instance can read it. Deleting the session logs the user out immediately.
entries.detail: Revocability is the main advantage over a JWT, which stays valid until it expires.

entries.short: Self-contained signed claims, verified without a lookup.
entries.medium: The server verifies the signature and trusts the claims, which scales well and works across services. The cost is that it is valid until expiry, so early revocation needs a denylist or short lifetimes.
entries.detail: Never store secrets in a JWT payload. It is signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read it.

entries.short: Short access token plus a revocable refresh token.
entries.medium: The access token is short-lived for cheap verification. The refresh token is long-lived and stored server-side so it can be revoked. Logout revokes the refresh token, and the access token dies on its own soon after.
entries.detail: Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so script cannot read it.

entries.short: Agree on resources, shapes and errors up front.
entries.medium: Define the resources and the exact request and response shapes, then share types or generate a typed client so the two sides cannot drift. Design endpoints around what the UI needs, not around tables.
entries.detail: The error shape and loading states are part of the contract too. The client needs to tell empty from not-loaded.

entries.short: The server decides; the client only hides.
entries.medium: Check ownership and role on the server for every request, including object-level checks so a user cannot read another user's record by changing an id. Hiding a button in the UI is not access control.
entries.detail: Broken object-level authorization is one of the most common real-world API vulnerabilities.

entries.medium: A monolith gives transactions, one deploy and simple debugging. Microservices give independent scaling and team autonomy at the cost of distributed data, network failure and more operations.
entries.detail: Start with a modular monolith and extract a service when it actually needs to scale or be owned separately.

entries.short: The same value can be cached in five places.
entries.medium: Browser, edge, application, database and client state. A write usually invalidates the database but not the rest, so a stale copy survives wherever the read hits first.
entries.detail: Invalidate every layer on write, prefer deleting entries over updating them, and use cache tags to purge precisely.

entries.short: Slow follow-up work belongs in a queue.
entries.medium: Email, reports, image processing and notifications should be enqueued so the request returns fast. A worker handles them and can retry, with a dead-letter queue for repeated failures.
entries.detail: This is the difference between a snappy request and one that blocks on a third party.

entries.short: In a distributed system, some calls will fail.
entries.medium: Every network call needs a timeout, retries with backoff for transient failures, and a circuit breaker to stop hammering a failing dependency. Degrade gracefully rather than failing the whole request.
entries.detail: Idempotent writes make retries safe. Without that, a retry can double-charge or double-create.

entries.short: Presentation on the client, rules and secrets on the server.
entries.medium: Keep authorization, business rules and secrets on the server. Keep presentation, interaction and caching on the client. Decide this boundary deliberately, because it determines what you can trust.
entries.detail: Anything shipped to the browser is public, so no secret or rule that matters can live only there.

entries.short: Logs, metrics and traces across every hop.
entries.medium: A request crosses many components, so a correlation id that travels with it ties the logs together. Metrics catch trends, traces show where time goes, and alerts catch the rest.
entries.detail: Without a shared id, debugging a full-stack issue means guessing which component to look at first.
